text: Mammoth Cave National Park is a U.S. national park located in south-central Kentucky, encompassing 52,007 acres (21,046 ha) primarily in Edmonson County, with small portions extending into Hart and Barren counties. The park includes the longest known cave system in the world, the Mammoth–Flint Ridge Cave System, which was formally named in 1972 after a connection was discovered between Mammoth Cave and the longer Flint Ridge system. As of 2025, more than 426 miles (686 km) of passageways have been surveyed, exceeding the length of Mexico's Sac Actun cave system by over 1.5 times. The park was established on July 1, 1941, following contentious eminent domain proceedings that continue to impact the region. It was designated a World Heritage Site on October 27, 1981, an International Biosphere Reserve on September 26, 1990, and an International Dark Sky Park on October 28, 2021. The park’s mission, as stated in its foundation document, is to preserve, protect, interpret, and study the internationally recognized biological and geologic features, including the cave system, the forested karst landscape, the Green and Nolin rivers, and evidence of human history, while providing public enjoyment, recreation, and understanding. The cave developed in Mississippian-aged limestone capped by the Big Clifty Sandstone, which has made the system stable; thin limestone layers within the sandstone create an epikarstic zone where tiny conduits dissolve due to acidic groundwater, leading to surface springs that later sink underground at the sandstone-limestone contact. The underlying limestone layers, in order from top to bottom, are the Girkin Formation, Ste. Genevieve Limestone, and St. Louis Limestone; the Main Cave passage is located at the base of the Girkin and top of the Ste. Genevieve. The cave’s stratigraphy is studied through correlation with explorer surveys to produce approximate three-dimensional maps without drilling. The sandstone caprock resists water penetration except through vertical cracks, making many upper passages dry and lacking stalactites or stalagmites, though erosion has created exceptions like the Frozen Niagara room. The contact between sandstone and limestone is visible when hiking from valley bottoms to ridgetops, where rock composition shifts from limestone to sandstone at a defined elevation. A massive sinkhole known as Cedar Sink exists in the southern part of the park, where a small river enters and disappears underground. The National Park Service offers several cave tours, including lighted tours of one to six hours featuring features like Grand Avenue, Frozen Niagara, and Fat Man's Misery, as well as two tours using only paraffin lamps. "Wild" tours explore remote, muddy, or dusty areas. The Echo River Tour, which involved boat rides along an underground river, was discontinued in the early 1990s due to logistical and environmental concerns. The park’s headquarters and visitor center are located on Mammoth Cave Parkway, accessible directly from I-65 at Exit 48, which connects with Kentucky Route 70 from the north and Kentucky Route 255 from the south. Human activity in the cave dates back five thousand years, with Native American remains, including mummies, recovered in the 19th and 20th centuries, reflecting intentional burial practices. In 1935, the remains of an adult male, named "Lost John," were found under a boulder after a pre-Columbian miner disturbed the rubble; the remains were publicly exhibited until the 1970s when they were interred in a secret location for preservation and political sensitivity. Research beginning in the late 1950s by Patty Jo Watson of Washington University in St. Louis used carbon dating and dietary analysis of preserved specimens to determine that the region’s Archaic and early Woodland peoples transitioned from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture. Experimental archaeology, where modern explorers used ancient tools, helped researchers understand the challenges faced by early cave users. Artifacts such as cane torches, drawings, gourd fragments, and woven grass moccasin slippers are found in Salts Cave in the Flint Ridge system. The 31,000-acre "Pollard Survey" was sold by indenture on September 10, 1791, in Philadelphia by William Pollard; 19,897 acres between Bacon Creek and the Green River were purchased by Thomas Lang Jr. on June 3, 1796, for £4,116.65, and were later lost to a county tax claim during the War of 1812. Legend attributes the first European visit to Mammoth Cave to either John or Francis Houchin in 1797, though John Decatur "Johnny Dick" Houchin, who was only 10 years old, is unlikely to have been involved; Francis "Frank" Houchin is more probable due to his proximity to the cave entrance, though Charles Houchin, a hunter, may have shot the bear that led to the discovery. Brucker and Watson’s work suggests the cave was known before 1797. Valentine Simon first surveyed and registered the land in 1798 and began exploiting the cave for saltpeter. During the War of 1812, increased demand due to the Jefferson Embargo Act of 1807 led to a surge in saltpeter production, making cave mining profitable. In July 1812, Charles Wilkins and Hyman Gratz purchased the cave and began industrial-scale mining of calcium nitrate using 70 enslaved laborers to build and operate leaching apparatus and haul soil. A half-interest in the cave was sold for $10,000 (equivalent to over $150,000 in 2020). After the war, mining ceased and the cave became a minor tourist attraction centered on a nearby Native American mummy. Wilkins’ estate sold his interest to Gratz, and in 1838, the Gratz brothers sold the cave to Franklin Gorin, who intended to operate it as a tourist attraction. Gorin was a slave owner who used enslaved people as guides; Stephen Bishop, one of them, became a celebrated guide, making extensive maps and naming many cave features. Gorin wrote that Bishop was the first to cross the Bottomless Pit and the only person known to have reached the bottom of Gorin’s Dome. After Bishop’s discovery, interest shifted from the "Old Cave" to new areas, which Bishop described as "grand, gloomy and peculiar." In 1839, John Croghan of Louisville purchased the estate, including Bishop and other slaves. Croghan briefly operated a tuberculosis hospital in the cave in 1842–43, believing the cave’s vapors would cure patients, but the disease ultimately killed him in 1849. In 1866, Charles Waldack, a photographer from Cincinnati, took the first photos inside the cave using magnesium flash photography. Throughout the 19th century, Mammoth Cave gained international fame, attracting writers such as Robert Montgomery Bird, Robert Davidson, Horace Martin, Alexander Clark Bullitt, Nathaniel Parker Willis, Bayard Taylor, William Stump Forwood, and John Muir. Famous visitors included actor Edwin Booth (brother of John Wilkes Booth, who assassinated Lincoln in 1865), singer Jenny Lind (who visited on April 5, 1851), and violinist Ole Bull, who gave a concert in the cave; two chambers are now known as "Booth's Amphitheatre" and "Ole Bull's Concert Hall." The difficult farming conditions in the region led to commercial exploitation of nearby caves, resulting in the "Kentucky Cave Wars," a period of intense competition where private cave owners used deception—such as misleading signs or "cappers" who falsely claimed Mammoth Cave was closed—to lure tourists. In 1906, Mammoth Cave became accessible by steamboat with the construction of a lock and dam at Brownsville, Kentucky. In 1908, Max Kämper, a German mining engineer, arrived from New York and spent several months exploring the cave with the help of Ed Bishop. He produced an accurate instrumental survey of many kilometers of the cave and a corresponding surface topographic map, which was suppressed by the Croghan family and is no longer known, though the cave map remains a significant achievement in cave cartography. Kämper speculated that Mammoth Cave was connected to Salts and Colossal Caves, a connection not proven until 60 years later. In the early 1920s, George Morrison created new entrances to Mammoth Cave via blasting on land not owned by the Croghans. Without access to the Croghan family’s unpublished surveys, it was proven that they had been exhibiting cave sections not on their land, leading to lawsuits and competition among entrances. Floyd Collins spent ten years exploring the Flint Ridge Cave System, discovering Floyd Collins' Crystal Cave and exploring Salts Cave, before dying in 1925 at Sand Cave after dislodging a rock on his leg and being unable to be rescued due to starvation. The rescue attempts generated widespread media attention and contributed to a movement that led to the establishment of Mammoth Cave National Park in 1941. As the last Croghan heirs passed away, advocacy grew among wealthy Kentuckians, who formed the Mammoth Cave National Park Association in 1924. The park was authorized on May 25, 192.

The geographic extent of Mammoth Cave revealed that the Croghans had long been exhibiting sections of the cave not owned by them, leading to lawsuits and the operation of different cave entrances in direct competition. In the early 20th century, Floyd Collins spent ten years exploring the Flint Ridge Cave System, during which he discovered Floyd Collins' Crystal Cave and explored Salts Cave, before dying in 1925 at Sand Cave, Kentucky, after dislodging a rock onto his leg during a tight crawlway and being unable to be rescued due to starvation. Rescue attempts generated widespread media attention, prompting prominent Kentuckians to form a movement that led to the establishment of Mammoth Cave National Park in 1941. As the last Croghan heirs passed away, advocacy grew among wealthy Kentucky citizens, who formed the Mammoth Cave National Park Association in 1924, and the park was authorized on May 25, 1926. Donated funds were used to purchase farmsteads, while other land within the proposed park boundary was acquired via eminent domain, displacing thousands of people and resulting in bitter disputes with inadequate compensation, a situation that received little outside attention. The federal government was legally barred from restoring or developing cleared farmsteads while the private Association held the land, a restriction evaded by operating a maximum of four CCC camps from May 22, 1933 to July 1942. According to the National Park Service, by May 22, 1936, 27,402 acres (11,089 ha) had been acquired and accepted, and the area was officially declared a national park on July 1, 1941, when a minimum of 45,310 acres (18,340 ha), comprising over 600 parcels, had been assembled. Superintendent Hoskins noted that a summer tanager named Pete arrived at the guide house around April 20 each year starting in 1938, eating from guides' hands and feeding his mate, delighting visitors. Mammoth Cave National Park was dedicated on July 1, 1941, and the same year saw the incorporation of the National Speleological Society. R. Taylor Hoskins, the second Acting Superintendent under the old Association, became the first official Superintendent and served until 1951. The New Entrance, closed since 1941, was reopened on December 26, 1951, becoming the starting point for the Frozen Niagara tour. By 1954, the park's land holdings included all lands within its outer boundary except for two privately held tracts; one, the old Lee Collins farm, was sold to Harry Thomas of Horse Cave, Kentucky, whose grandson William "Bill" Austin operated Collins Crystal Cave as a show cave in direct competition with the park, which maintained roads to the property. In February 1954, a two-week expedition under the National Speleological Society, known as C-3 or the Collins Crystal Cave Expedition, was organized at Austin's invitation. The expedition drew public interest through a photo essay by Robert Halmi in the July 1954 issue of True Magazine and a double first-person account by Joe Lawrence Jr. and Roger Brucker, confirming that passages in Crystal Cave extended toward Mammoth Cave proper, exceeding its boundaries, though the explorers kept this information secret due to fears of park restrictions. In 1955, Crystal Cave was connected by survey to Unknown Cave, the first connection in the Flint Ridge system. Some C-3 participants wished to continue exploring and formed the Flint Ridge Reconnaissance under Austin, Jim Dyer, John J. Lehrberger, and E. Robert Pohl, which was incorporated in 1957 as the Cave Research Foundation to support academic and scientific research; notable researchers included Patty Jo Watson. In March 1961, the Crystal Cave property was sold to the National Park Service for $285,000, and the Great Onyx Cave property, the only other private inholding, was purchased for $365,000; the Cave Research Foundation was allowed to continue exploration through a Memorandum of Understanding with the National Park Service. In 1960, Colossal Cave was connected to Salts Cave, and in 1961, Colossal-Salts was connected to Crystal-Unknown, forming a single cave system under much of Flint Ridge. By 1972, the Flint Ridge Cave System had been surveyed to 86.5 miles (139.2 km), making it the longest cave in the world. During the 1960s, CRF teams found passages in the Flint Ridge system that penetrated under Houchins Valley and came within 800 feet (240 m) of known Mammoth Cave passages. In 1972, CRF Chief Cartographer John Wilcox led expeditions from the Flint Ridge side and explored leads in Mammoth Cave to connect the systems. On a July 1972 trip, Patricia Crowther, weighing 115 pounds (52 kg), crawled through a narrow canyon called the "Tight Spot," a filter for larger cavers. On August 30, 1972, Wilcox, Crowther, Richard Zopf, and Tom Brucker passed through the Tight Spot and discovered the name "Pete H" inscribed on a river passage wall with an arrow pointing toward Mammoth Cave, believed to have been carved by Warner P. "Pete" Hanson, who died in World War II; the passage was named Hanson's Lost River. On September 9, 1972, a six-person CRF team—Wilcox, Crowther, Zopf, Gary Eller, Stephen Wells, and Cleveland Pinnix (a National Park Service ranger)—followed Hanson's Lost River downstream to its connection with Echo River in Cascade Hall of Mammoth Cave, completing the connection between the Flint Ridge and Mammoth Cave systems, an achievement known as the "Everest of speleology," resulting in a surveyed system of 144.4 miles (232.4 km) with fourteen entrances. Further connections followed, including to Proctor/Morrison Cave beneath Joppa Ridge in 1979; Proctor Cave was discovered by Jonathan Doyle during the Civil War and later owned by the Mammoth Cave Railroad, and Morrison Cave by George Morrison in the 1920s. This connection extended the frontier of Mammoth Cave exploration southeastward. Simultaneously, an independent group, the Central Kentucky Karst Coalition (CKKC), made discoveries outside the park, surveying tens of miles in Roppel Cave east of the park, discovered in 1976, which briefly ranked as one of the nation's longest caves before being connected to the Proctor/Morrison section on September 10, 1983, by a joint CRF and CKKC expedition entering through separate entrances and meeting in the middle. The resulting surveyed length reached nearly 300 miles (480 km). On March 19, 2005, a connection into the Roppel Cave portion was surveyed from a small cave under Eudora Ridge, adding about three miles; the entrance, now called the "Hoover Entrance," was discovered in September 2003 by Alan Canon and James Wells. Incremental discoveries since then have increased the total length to over 400 miles (640 km). It is certain that many more miles of cave passages remain undiscovered, with new natural entrances being rare and discovery primarily occurring through routine exploration of side passages from known entrances. At least two other major cave systems lie near Mammoth Cave: the Fisher Ridge Cave System, discovered in January 1981 by Michigan cavers associated with the Detroit Urban Grotto, mapped to 131 miles (211 km), and the Whigpistle Cave System, discovered in 1976 by Rick Schwartz, which connected to three nearby caves—Whigpistle, Martin Ridge, and Jackpot—now mapped to 42 miles (68 km) as of 2025, with ongoing exploration. Located 7 miles (11 km) from the visitor center is Diamond Caverns, where a stagecoach used to ferry visitors from the Bells Tavern train stop in Park City, Kentucky, to both Diamond Caverns and Mammoth Cave is on display. The park has a Humid subtropical climate (Cfa) according to the Köppen classification, and the Plant Hardiness zone at the visitor center, at 722 ft (220 m) elevation, is 6b with an average annual extreme minimum temperature of -3.2°F (-19.6°C). Bats inhabiting the caverns include the Indiana bat (Myotis sodalis), gray bat (Myotis grisescens), little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus), big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus), and tricolored bat (Perimyotis subflavus); rare species like the eastern small-footed bat have estimated populations of 9–12 million in the Historic Section, though numbers are now only a few thousand, and ecological restoration to support bat populations is ongoing. The red bat (Lasiurus borealis) is a forest-dweller and rarely found underground. Other cave animals include three species of cave crickets (Hadenoecus subterraneus, Ceuthophilus stygius, Ceuthophilus latens), a cave beetle (Pseudanophthalmus inexpectatus), fishing spiders (Dolomedes spp.), a cave salamander (Eurycea lucifuga), two eyeless cavefish (Typhlichthys subterraneus and Amblyopsis spelaea), a cave crayfish (Orconectes pellucidus), and the Kentucky cave shrimp (Palaemonias ganteri); some surface animals may use cave entrances but do not enter deep passages. The Green River flowing through the park is legally designated as "Kentucky Wild River" by the Kentucky General Assembly through the Office of Kentucky Nature Preserves' Wild Rivers Program. The park's potential natural vegetation type is Oak/Hickory (100) with an Eastern Hardwood Temperate broadleaf and mixed forest (25) form. Common fossils include crinoids, blastoids, and gastropods; Mississippian limestone has yielded fossils of over a dozen shark species, including part of a Saivodus striatus, comparable in size to a modern great white shark, and the species Glikmanius careforum and Troglocladodus trimblei, known only from within the cave. The cave's name refers to the large width and length of passages near the Rotunda entrance and was used long before the full system was explored, with no woolly mammoth fossils ever found, meaning the name has no connection to the extinct mammal. Brucker has co-authored four nonfiction books and authored one historical novel on the Mammoth Cave System, presented here in the order of the events in their narratives, not publication order. Kenneth C. Carstens authored two academic works: "Archaeological Investigations in the Central Kentucky Karst" (1980, 2 vols.) and "Archaeological Reconnaissance in Mammoth Cave National Park" (1973), both from the Department of Anthropology at Washington University in St. Louis.
